turns.prompt_text: I like learning about statistics, I'd like to find a javascript statistics visualization library with a good variety, I have found amcharts.org, which I find very diverse with a good variety, however it is extremely expensive for my use case
turns.response_html:
amCharts is beautiful and incredibly feature-rich, but the commercial licensing costs can definitely be a barrier for independent projects or smaller budgets.

If you want a free, open-source alternative that matches amCharts in variety—especially for statistical and complex visualization—here are the top contenders to look into, depending on what flavor of implementation you prefer:

1. Plotly.js (The Best for Deep Statistics)

If your primary focus is statistics, Plotly.js is arguably the closest free open-source match to the sheer diversity of amCharts.

  • The Vibe: It abstracts heavy scientific and statistical charts (similar to what you'd see in Python's matplotlib or ggplot2).
  • Variety: Over 40 chart types out of the box. Beyond standard bars and lines, it handles box plots, 2D density plots, error bars, parallel coordinates, violin plots, and full 3D mathematical graphing via WebGL.
  • License: MIT (Completely free for commercial and personal use).

2. Apache ECharts (The Best for amCharts-Style Polished UI)

Originally built by Baidu and now managed by the Apache Foundation, ECharts is a massive, incredibly powerful library that matches amCharts' aesthetic out of the box.

  • The Vibe: Highly animated, responsive, customizable, and capable of handling huge datasets using HTML5 Canvas and WebGL.
  • Variety: It features comprehensive statistical charting, customizable heatmaps, multi-axis relations, tree-maps, sunbursts, and excellent geo-spatial mapping.
  • License: Apache 2.0 (Free for commercial use).

3. Observable Plot / D3.js (The Best for Custom Exploratory Data)

If you want to construct bespoke statistical graphics using a modern "Grammar of Graphics" approach, the team behind D3 created Observable Plot.

  • The Vibe: Instead of choosing rigid "chart types," you layer geometric shapes (marks), scales, and data transforms.
  • Variety: Infinite, because you build what you need. It includes incredibly elegant native data transforms for binning quantitative values, computing rolling averages, and faceting data into small multiples.
  • License: ISC (Free and open-source).

4. ApexCharts (The Best for Clean Dashboards)

If you don't need highly niche scientific plots but want standard statistical dashboards that look extremely modern and elegant, ApexCharts is a fantastic drop-in replacement.

  • The Vibe: Crisp SVG rendering, beautiful default color palettes, and great interactive zoom/pan capabilities.
  • Variety: Great handling of scatter plots, heatmaps, mixed charts (e.g., line + column), timeline/gantt styles, and radar profiles.
  • License: MIT.

Summary Recommendation

If you need...Go with...
Pure statistical variety (Violin plots, Box plots, 3D math)Plotly.js
Rich, interactive amCharts look-and-feel + massive datasetsApache ECharts
To design completely custom data visualizations from scratchObservable Plot
A beautiful dashboard setup with zero design effortApexCharts

Are you looking to build a specific type of statistical chart (like a distribution histogram, correlation matrix, or regression trend line), or are you focusing on a particular frontend framework?

Assuming you mean a Gantt chart (for tracking timelines, schedules, and project dependencies), amCharts does them beautifully, but you can absolutely build them for free with the open-source libraries we just looked at!

Here is how the top free options handle Gantt and timeline tracking:

1. Apache ECharts (Best for Complex, Interactive Gantt Charts)

ECharts doesn't have a rigid "Gantt" component name; instead, it uses a Custom Series or a Bar Chart with a transparent base to map start and end dates.

  • Capabilities: Highly interactive. It supports drag-and-drop updating, multi-level grouping (e.g., grouping tasks under specific teams), progress bars inside the data blocks, and zoomable timelines.
  • Look and Feel: Smooth animations and easily handles hundreds of parallel tasks without breaking a sweat.

2. ApexCharts (Easiest to Set Up out of the Box)

If you want a classic, clean Gantt chart with almost zero configuration, ApexCharts has native support via its Range Bar Chart.

  • Capabilities: You pass it a y (the task name) and an array of two coordinates for x (the start and end timestamps). It automatically formats the time axis, supports grouped rows, and handles overlapping timelines perfectly.
  • Look and Feel: Modern, flat UI that looks like a sleek SaaS dashboard right out of the box.

3. Plotly.js (Best for Milestone & Resource Mapping)

Plotly handles Gantt charts natively using its figure_factory or via a horizontal bar chart utilizing a base offset for the start times.

  • Capabilities: Excellent for displaying project milestones, tracking resource allocation (who is working on what), and showing percentage completion via color gradients.
  • Look and Feel: Highly precise, data-dense, and comes with built-in hover tooltips and panning tools.

Code Example: Quick ApexCharts Gantt

To see how lightweight a free option can be, here is how you define a basic Gantt timeline in ApexCharts:

var options = {
  series: [
    {
      data: [
        { x: 'Design Phase', y: [new Date('2026-07-01').getTime(), new Date('2026-07-15').getTime()] },
        { x: 'Frontend Dev', y: [new Date('2026-07-12').getTime(), new Date('2026-08-10').getTime()] },
        { x: 'Backend Dev',  y: [new Date('2026-07-15').getTime(), new Date('2026-08-20').getTime()] },
        { x: 'Testing & QA', y: [new Date('2026-08-18').getTime(), new Date('2026-09-01').getTime()] }
      ]
    }
  ],
  chart: { type: 'rangeBar', height: 350 },
  plotOptions: { bar: { horizontal: true } },
  xaxis: { type: 'datetime' }
};

var chart = new ApexCharts(document.querySelector("#chart"), options);
chart.render();

If your project requires advanced features like task dependency lines (arrows drawing from one task to the next showing what blocks what), Frappe Gantt is another tiny, specialized open-source library built strictly for Gantt charts that might be worth a look!
